READING 49
EQUITY ANALYST RESEARCH
REPORTS
MODULE 49.1: EQUITY ANALYST RESEARCH
REPORTS
LOS 49.a: Describe the elements that should be covered in a detailed
company research report.
A company research report includes an analyst’s valuation and investment
recommendations, based on analysis of the current and forecast company
performance and position.
An initial research report for external distribution (said to be initiating coverage
of a company) is likely to be thorough, followed by subsequent updates that are
less thorough. These updates may be produced after widely anticipated events,
such as mergers or earnings releases.
The basic structure and key items typically included in an initial company
research report, with the intention of introducing the company to investors, are
as follows:
Front page. While presented first, the front page should be written last. The
front page should show the analyst’s buy/hold/sell recommendation and target
buying or selling prices. It should include an investment thesis that summarizes
the arguments supporting the analyst’s recommendation. Also on the front page
should be the subject company’s name, ticker symbol, primary sector and
industry, market capitalization and float, key recent developments, and a
summary of recent and forecast financial data, such as earnings. All of these
will then be covered in further detail in the remainder of the research report.
Analysis of the business model. This section introduces the company to the
reader. It will cover how the firm generates value, including revenue drivers

(e.g., which products or services are offered, pricing strategies, major
customers) and expense drivers (e.g., major suppliers, distribution strategies).
Industry overview and competitive positioning. The analyst producing the
report may have industry expertise, but he should not assume that the reader
does, so introducing the industry is important. Many firms choose not to
explicitly name their competitors, so it is up to the analyst to establish which
companies should be considered as peers. Industry analysis should incorporate
quantitative comparisons, such as market capitalization, P/E multiples,
earnings growth, and return figures—as well as qualitative analysis using
models such as PESTLE and Porter’s five forces. Full analysis of these models
does not necessarily need to be included in the research report; the analyst
should apply discretion in including only the pertinent information. For
example, the technological element of PESTLE analysis will be crucial in
industries like telecommunications, but less important in others, such as basic
materials.
Financial analysis and valuation. The analyst will conduct thorough financial
analysis of the company, but the research report does not necessarily need an
exhaustive commentary on the financial statements. It should include only
those measures and financial ratios (general or industry specific) that are
relevant for supporting the analyst’s price target. Applying a critical eye to
which information to include is increasingly important in an age where AI can
produce seemingly endless amounts of financial analysis at the press of a
button.
Using financial statements (including footnotes and disclosures) and other
information, the analyst will use both actual past performance and forecast
performance to produce a price target. Forecast performance will be based on
company-specific factors as well as the wider industry and economy, focusing
on any specific short-term or long-term catalysts the analyst identifies as
relevant. The analyst will likely use various valuation techniques to calculate
the intrinsic value of a company’s equity shares, then use it to identify a price
target. The target can be an absolute monetary amount or stated against a
benchmark, such as an index, industry average, or the analyst’s universe of
companies. The price target may be a point estimate or a range and typically
covers a period of one to two years.
Investment risks. This section provides further detail on key risks the analyst
identified in the section on valuation. These risks may be company specific,

industry specific, or related to the wider economy. Some may be related to the
quantitative analysis used in the valuation models, such as sensitivity to the
analyst’s assumptions.
Environmental, social, and governance factors. The content of this section may
vary depending on the industry or countries in which the company operates,
but it may be crucial in industries such as air travel or data storage, where
environmental concerns have increasing importance.
Recommendation. The research report must reach a conclusion and recommend
a trading action for the stock. Buy, sell, or hold is the most common
terminology. Some firms use overweight, underweight, and neutral with the
same meanings. The analyst will consider all information gathered when
reaching their conclusion.
No single approach can determine where a hold recommendation turns into a
buy or sell. However, a rough guide is to assign a buy recommendation if a stock
is expected to appreciate at least 10%-15% on an absolute basis or relative to a
benchmark; a sell recommendation if the stock is expected to decline at least
10%-15%; or a hold recommendation for anything in between.
Key items typically included in a subsequent company research report are as
follows:
Front matter (similar to what was described previously, but more condensed)
Recommendation, including rationales for changes
Analysis of new information (e.g., updated financial statements, variance
analysis of expected vs. actual results)
Changes to the initial valuation, with supporting rationales
Changes in risks since the initial or most recent report
Regardless of the type of research report produced, maintaining the highest level
of ethical and analytical standards is paramount. A well-written, timely report
should distinguish clearly between facts and opinions, disclose any potential
conflicts of interest the analyst or firm may have, and provide adequate
information about risks an investor may face.
LOS 49.b: Compare sell-side and buy-side equity analyst reports and their
conclusions.

The main differences between a sell-side research report and a buy-side
research report are the entity that creates the report and the purpose of the
report.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
A common misconception is that sell-side reports give sell
recommendations, and buy-side reports give buy recommendations.
This is not the case. Sell-side and buy-side refer to the producers of the
report.
Sell-Side Research Reports
Sell-side research reports are typically produced by investment banks and are
created for their clients. These research reports can be used to support
relationships between the bank and its clients (e.g., in issuing or underwriting
debt and equity securities, increasing volumes for broker or dealer trading, or
advisory work).
Typically, the analyst producing the reports will have expertise in a specific
industry and focus on selected companies within that industry. However, unless
the research is directly sold, creating sell-side research reports incurs costs
without bringing in any revenue. Therefore, a sell-side firm needs to limit the
universe of companies its research analysts cover. Within an industry, a research
analyst must consider how many companies are feasible to cover, and which
ones have desirable characteristics for coverage.
High-quality ongoing coverage of a stock can benefit both the stock issuer and
the investment bank. Research coverage may lend credibility to a stock and
increase its trading volume, which helps to bring in commissions from trades for
the investment bank.
Investment banks have potential conflicts of interest if they provide other
services to a company, such as underwriting. The relevant teams face regulatory
constraints to ensure that research remains objective, and that research analysts
do not have access to any material nonpublic information that teams elsewhere
in the organization may hold. Regulations may also limit issuing research reports
close to an IPO or secondary equity offering, or may require research (if sold) to
be paid for by asset managers separately from any trade execution costs. While it
is common for sell-side research reports to give buy or hold recommendations
(or switch between the two), analysts may be reluctant to issue sell

recommendations if they perceive a risk that doing so will harm the firm’s
relationship with the company in question.
While some sell-side research reports may present views contrary to the market
consensus, this requires a high degree of certainty on the part of the analyst, so it
is more typical for sell-side recommendations to be in line with the consensus.
Because platforms such as Bloomberg often show select information from
analysts such as forecast profit margins, it is straightforward to obtain
information about the market consensus.
Buy-Side Research Reports
The buy side refers primarily to firms that invest in securities. Unlike sell-side
reports, buy-side research is typically confidential and is used internally by a
firm’s investment committee to support investment decisions or monitor existing
positions. Buy-side analysts write their own reports, but they will often use
publicly available sell-side reports to enhance their knowledge of a particular
company. Using these sell-side reports does not necessarily mean the buy-side
analyst will reach the same investment recommendation.
Without the pressure of considering potential trading volumes and potential
commissions, buy-side research generally has more scope to focus on smaller
stocks, should the analyst see fit.
Buy-side firms engage in stock screening to narrow the universe of equities to
which they will devote research resources. Increasingly, they use finance
software, AI, and platforms such as Bloomberg to assist with stock screening.
The initial level of screening determines the universe of stocks (e.g., a specific
index). Next, the firm applies quantitative criteria, such as growth rates and
profit margins, alongside any other metrics that fit the desired investment
strategy. The firm refines these criteria until the appropriate number of stocks
remain, which the firm’s research analysts can cover with appropriate depth.
Equity analysts should, however, be aware that any arbitrary criterion set (e.g., a
specific profit margin) may result in an appealing stock being omitted.
One branch of buy-side research is activist short selling. This is typically
carried out by small equity analyst teams and focuses on stocks the analysts
believe are likely to decline significantly in value. The analysts look to uncover
misinformation in the market that is inflating the market price, or undiscovered
fraud which, once made public, will reduce the stock price significantly. In

contrast with most buy-side research, which remains internal and confidential,
activist short sellers often circulate their research publicly after they have
released it to their limited partner investors.
Sell-side research reports have the following characteristics:
Objective. The objective is to provide information and recommendations to
clients.
Level of analysis and detail. Sell-side analysts cover a wide range of industries
and stocks for a diverse audience, but they tend to use a standardized format.
Target audience. External investors and traders are the main target audience for
sell-side research.
Valuation methods. Methods include discounted cash flow, multiples, and other
common models, focusing on future earnings.
Regulatory constraints. Constraints include regulations dealing with conflicts
of interest due to additional relationships with covered companies and
investment banking clients.
Buy-side research reports have the following characteristics:
Objective. The objective is to support internal decision-making.
Level of analysis and detail. Reports are customized and in depth, with a
specific focus on stocks or industries.
Target audience. The target audiences are internal investment teams and
portfolio managers.
Valuation methods. Analysts might use models created internally at their firms
in addition to traditional valuation methods.
Regulatory constraints. These reports are mostly unregulated, as the
information is typically not made public.
LOS 49.c: Explain why value estimates from the same modeling approach
may differ based on analyst assumptions regarding revenue, profitability,
investment, and financing.
Valuation models require several estimates or forecasts, which can lead to
differing outcomes for different analysts. One analyst may estimate an intrinsic
value that is above the current market value and provide a buy recommendation,
while another analyst may value the same stock below the current market price

and provide a sell recommendation. This is not a weakness of the valuation
process; differing valuations encourage price discovery and efficient markets.
Differing price targets can also be due to other factors, such as location. A
domestic analyst may value a stock differently than a foreign analyst who might
see a particular firm as a good opportunity to gain exposure to a new market.
Stocks for which different analysts produce widely dispersed valuations are
known as hard-to-value stocks.
To understand what assumptions have been used, if not explicitly stated, one can
assume that an analyst’s price target is the intrinsic value estimated using a
discounted cash flow model, then solve for one of the underlying assumptions of
that model, such as long-term growth.

$46.50 per share. The firm has 10 million shares outstanding. Assuming the

$24 million, and a required return of 8%, calculate the long-term growth rate

Some key drivers for the range of valuations analysts may produce are estimated
revenue growth and its effect on profitability, as well as their assumptions
regarding terminal value and a company’s investment and financing
requirements.
Revenue and Profitability
Greater revenue growth is typically seen as an indicator of a higher-valued stock,
going hand-in-hand with higher free cash flow. However, looking at revenue
growth in isolation can be misleading. An analyst must consider the source of
changes in a company’s revenue and cash flow, such as changes in its cost
structure. The following example illustrates the different impacts of revenue and
cost changes on profit margins.
EXAMPLE: Evaluating the impact of cost structure assumptions
Deck Health, Inc., has released its most recent earnings, showing revenue for
20X6 at $10 million and operating profit of $4 million, giving an operating
profit margin of 40%. Three analysts update their forecasts for the next two

years. They all expect revenue to grow by 3% annually due to higher sales
volume, but they have differing opinions about how costs will change.
Analyst 1 assumes that operating costs will rise in line with revenue at 3% for
the next two years.
Analyst 2 assumes that costs will rise by 4% due to necessary operating
changes in the production processes, such as hiring additional staff.
Analyst 3 assumes that Deck Health will be able to achieve some economies of
scale by producing higher volumes, and that costs will only rise by 2% each
year.
Evaluate the impact the different assumptions have on Deck Health’s forecast
operating profit margin.
Answer:
Despite all three analysts forecasting the same revenue for 20X7 and 20X8, the
operating profit margin varies due to the different cost assumptions. Analyst 1,
who predicts costs to grow proportionally to revenue, has forecast a steady
40% operating profit margin. Analyst 2 has forecast a worsening operating

profit margin due to higher labor costs, while Analyst 3 believes economies of
scale will result in an increasing operating profit margin.
Capital Investment, Terminal Value, and Financing
Requirements
Analysts must consider a company’s investment needs when forecasting cash
flow. If growth in investment matches growth in net income, no overall change
in free cash flow results. If investment grows at a slower rate than income, the
forecast free cash flow will increase. While this may seem positive, an analyst
must ask whether growth in free cash flow is sustainable without significant
capital investment, and should be skeptical of long-term revenue or profitability
growth projections that are not backed up by investment in the capital needs of
the business. On the other hand, if a company is increasing investment and this is
not resulting in income growth, forecast free cash flow will decline, and the
company will produce a lower return on capital in the long run.
In most valuation models such as FCFE, a substantial portion of the value of the
business comes from the terminal value. An analyst should consider carefully
how long a forecast horizon can be forecast accurately and what assumptions,
such as growth rate, are built into the terminal value, as these can have a material
impact on the valuation produced.
While financing choices have some impact on valuation, they are less important
than factors that result from operating and strategic decisions. One should be
wary of a valuation that places a large emphasis on financing decisions.
MODULE QUIZ 49.1
1. Which of the following statements regarding company research reports subsequent to
initiating coverage is most accurate?
A. The report updates the recommendation in light of new information about the company.
B. The primary audience is those who are not already knowledgeable about the company
or security.
C. The report provides an industry overview and information on competitive positioning
and ESG considerations.
2. An analyst expects a stock to increase in value by 9%, while its benchmark index is
expected to grow by 6%. Which of the following recommendations from the analyst is
least likely?
A. Buy.
B. Sell.
C. Hold.

3. Which of the following equity analyst teams is most likely to create a research report on a
small, newly formed company that shows great potential?
A. Buy-side equity analysts.
B. Sell-side equity analysts.
C. Activist short sellers.
4. An analyst is creating a forecast for a new company. Using the prior year’s results as a
starting point, she estimates that for the next three years, revenue and operating costs
will grow at the same percentage per year, with a lower growth rate in capital investment.
All else equal, what does her forecast imply about the company’s operating profit margin
over the three years? The analyst is forecasting that the operating profit margin will:
A. increase.
B. decrease.
C. not change.
KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 49.a
Key items typically included in an initial company research report are as
follows:
Front page
Analysis of the business model
Industry overview and competitive positioning
Financial analysis and valuation
Investment risks
Environmental, social, and governance factors
Recommendation
Key items typically included in a subsequent company research report are as
follows:
Front matter
Recommendation, including rationales for changes
Analysis of new information
Changes to the initial valuation, with supporting rationales
Changes in risks since the initial or most recent report
LOS 49.b

Sell-side research reports are typically produced by investment banks and are
created for the investment bank’s clients. These research reports can be used to
support relationships between the bank and the clients.
Sell-side research reports have the following characteristics:
Objective. The objective is to provide information and recommendations to
clients.
Level of analysis and detail. Sell-side analysts cover a wide range of industries
and stocks for a diverse audience, but they tend to use a standardized format.
Target audience. External investors and traders are the main target audience for
sell-side research.
Valuation methods. Methods include discounted cash flow, multiples, and other
common models, focusing on future earnings.
Regulatory constraints. Constraints include regulations dealing with conflicts
of interest due to additional relationships with covered companies and
investment banking clients.
Buy-side research is typically confidential, used internally by the investment
committee to support investment decisions or monitor existing positions.
One branch of buy-side research is activist short selling. The analysts look to
uncover misinformation in the market that is inflating the market price, or
undiscovered fraud that, once made public, will decrease the stock price.
Buy-side research reports have the following characteristics:
Objective. The objective is to support internal decision-making.
Level of analysis and detail. Reports are customized and in depth, with a
specific focus on stocks and/or industries.
Target audience. The target audiences are internal investment teams and
portfolio managers.
Valuation methods. Analysts might use models created internally at their firms
in addition to traditional valuation methods.
Regulatory constraints. These reports are mostly unregulated, as the
information is typically not made public.
LOS 49.c

Valuation models require several estimates or forecasts that can lead to differing
valuations of the same stock. The main drivers of differences are assumptions
around revenue and profitability growth, terminal value, and capital investment
requirements. Financing choices may have some impact on valuation, but they
tend not to be as significant.
ANSWER KEY FOR MODULE QUIZ
Module Quiz 49.1
. A Subsequent research reports update the recommendation and rationale from
an initial research report. The primary audience for an initial company
report is an audience who is not already knowledgeable about the issuer or
security. (LOS 49.a)
. B It is unlikely based on the information given that the analyst would issue a
sell recommendation. Although the stock is not expected to appreciate by
the guideline 10%-15%, this is only a guideline, and it is expected to
outperform the benchmark index. It is possible, therefore, that the analyst
may issue a buy recommendation, or a hold. (LOS 49.a)
. A Buy-side analysts are more able to focus on smaller stocks. Sell-side
analyst research reports are typically a cost center, so factors such as
potential trading volumes need to be considered when deciding which
companies to provide research on, generally leading to a focus on larger
stocks. Buy-side analysts do not have these restrictions. Activist short
sellers focus their research on stocks that are expected to decline
significantly in value. (LOS 49.b)
. C Revenue growing at the same percentage per year as operating costs will
result in a steady operating profit margin. Capital investment will not have
an impact on operating profit margin, but it is a use of cash when
calculating FCFE. A lower growth rate of capital investment compared to
operating profit implies increasing FCFE, although the analyst should
question whether the profit growth is sustainable with low capital
investment. (LOS 49.c)
